newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: North Korean wind chills Seoul shares, currency.
newsitem.headline: North Korean wind chills Seoul shares, currency.

text.p: Rising tensions on the Korean peninsula following the shooting of a prominent North Korean defector depressed the Seoul bourse on Monday but analysts said they expected the market to recover soon.
"The attack chilled the market," analyst Hwang Chang-joong of brokerage LG Securities said.

Li Il-nam, a nephew of North Korean leader Kim Jong-il's ex-wife, was shot and critically wounded at the weekend by suspected North Korean agents near Seoul. Li, who defected to South Korea in 1982, was in a coma on Monday.
"It looks inevitable for the market to correct downwardly for the time being," Hwang said.
The stock market's main index fell 9.39 points, or 1.30 percent, to end Monday's thin trading at 712.93.

The South Korean currency plunged to a new, 84-month low of 880.00 won against the dollar but dealers said a growing balance of payments deficit and the U.S. unit's strength against other major currencies were more to blame than political unrest.
The exchange rate was the lowest since March 1990 when Seoul introduced the market average exchange rate system.
The central bank stepped in to sell dollars at 876.80 won at the opening but failed to slow the won's decline.

South Korean officials said the attack on Li appeared to be a warning to Seoul and potential asylum seekers after Hwang Jang-yop, a top advisor to North Korean leader Kim, sought political asylum at South Korea's mission in Beijing last week.
They said a desperate North Korea might stage terrorist attacks to stop North Koreans from fleeing.
Analyst Cha Hee-gun of Sunkyung Securities said any more attacks linked to North Korea could worsen the country's risk rating.
He said South Korean investors, who are used to inter-Korean confrontation, would soon return to the market, however.
The 1950-53 Korean War ended in a truce agreement, instead of a peace treaty, and the two Koreas still remain technically at war.
"Foreign investors remain cautious," said Choi Bum of C.S. First Boston. "But the shooting incident alone will not deal a big blow to the market."
Foreign exchange dealers agreed that rising tensions on the Korean peninsula would deal more blows to the currency.
But they said the main reason behind the won's current weakness was the country's gaping current acount deficit.
South Korea posted a record deficit of $23.72 billion in 1996, up sharply from a shortfall of $8.95 billion the previous year.
